newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt needs less bureaucracy to grow - IFC.
newsitem.headline: Egypt needs less bureaucracy to grow - IFC.

text.p: The International Finance Corporation (IFC) chief said on Wednesday that Egypt must set its sights on luring a stream of foreign investment and cutting bureaucratic procedures if it wants to expand the economy.

Jannik Lindbaek, IFC executive vice president, told a news conference that capital inflows to the private sector would give Egypt's economy, currently growing at less than six percent a year, more scope to develop but only if the funds are properly utilised.

"Egypt is getting quite a bit of capital inflows but they are relatively small and there is a large need to create jobs and a tremendous need for continuous and strong economic growth," Lindbaek said.
"This is where the private sector has potential so Egypt's major goal should be attracting investment over the coming years and also to improve its absorption," he said.
The IFC, a member of the World Bank Group, says it is the largest source for equity and loan financing for private sector projects in developing countries.
In 1997, the corporation said it had approved $117 million of financing to Egypt and added it expected to invest another $150 to $200 million a year in the economy.
But Lindbaek said Egypt must deregulate its burgeoning bureaucracy it if wants to draw in more capital.
"Implementation of investment needs to be made easier, permits more available and all procedures to attract foreign investors in particular made more feasible," he said.

Investors have for years complained about being bogged down in red tape. But this month Egypt's parliament ratified a draft investment law which gives tax breaks of five to 20 years, aims to cut the lengthy procedures needed to set up a business and allows the government to give away land to investors in specified sectors.

Lindbaek also said the private sector should have a larger role to play in the infrastructure and tourism sectors as well as in finance -- areas from which the state is only just beginning to relinquish its monopoly.
"There's no reason why these sectors should not get much more than they already are getting and the state would benefit from the private sector in that respect," he added.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak appointed a new cabinet in 1996 which has accelerated economic reforms that for years had languished in government offices.

But while some analysts say the reforms are not going as quickly as they should, others say the government has shown that it is at least trying and that investment grade credit rating by rating firm Standard and Poor's prove it.

Privatisation is the flagship of these reforms. The state has said it aimed at speeding up the sale of its firms and has even talked about offering private investors a stake in one of its four main retail banks.

Last week, the cabinet also gave another boost to the private sector's role in the telecommunications sector by approving plans for private investors to take part in a mobile telephone company through a public offering.
